topics.title: Structure & Bonding
topics.concept:
Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds, and almost everything about how a molecule behaves follows from how its atoms are connected. Carbon has four valence electrons and completes its octet by forming four bonds. A Lewis structure shows this sharing: lines are bonding pairs and dots are lone pairs. You can check a structure's charge with formal charge = (valence electrons) − (lone-pair electrons) − ½(bonding electrons).

Hybridization explains molecular shape. When carbon forms four single bonds, it uses four equivalent sp³ orbitals arranged tetrahedrally, with bond angles of 109.5° (methane, CH₄). A carbon with a double bond is sp² hybridized: three orbitals lie in a plane 120° apart (trigonal planar) and one unhybridized p orbital forms the π bond (ethene, C₂H₄). A carbon with a triple bond is sp hybridized and linear at 180° (ethyne, C₂H₂). Lone pairs also matter: nitrogen in ammonia (NH₃) is sp³ with a ~107° angle, and oxygen in water (H₂O) is sp³ with a ~104.5° angle, because lone pairs occupy more space and squeeze the bonds together.

Bond polarity comes from electronegativity — an atom's pull on shared electrons. On the Pauling scale, the key values are F 4.0, O 3.5, N 3.0, Cl 3.2, C 2.5, and H 2.2. A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar covalent: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge (δ−) and the other a partial positive charge (δ+). The size of the difference tells you how polar the bond is, which in turn helps predict reactivity and whether a molecule has a net dipole moment.

questions.prompt: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in methane (CH₄)?
questions.explanation: Methane's carbon forms four single bonds, so it has four electron groups. Four groups = sp³ hybridization, which gives a tetrahedral geometry.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate H–C–H bond angle around a tetrahedral (sp³) carbon?
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral geometry places the four bonds as far apart as possible, giving 109.5° bond angles.

questions.prompt: Each carbon in ethene (C₂H₄) is sp² hybridized. What shape does this produce around each carbon?
questions.explanation: sp² gives three orbitals in a plane 120° apart (trigonal planar). The remaining unhybridized p orbital forms the π bond of the C=C double bond.

questions.prompt: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element (about 4.0). The order is F > O (3.5) > N (3.0) > C (2.5).

questions.prompt: What is the hybridization of each carbon atom in ethyne (HC≡CH)?
questions.explanation: Ethyne has a C≡C triple bond. Each carbon has two electron groups (one σ bond to the other carbon and one to hydrogen), so it is sp hybridized and linear at 180°.

questions.prompt: How many valence electrons does a neutral carbon atom have?
questions.explanation: Carbon is in group 14, so it has four valence electrons and forms four bonds to complete its octet.

questions.prompt: What is the formal charge on the nitrogen atom in NH₄⁺ (ammonium)?
questions.explanation: Formal charge = valence − (lone-pair electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons, 0 lone pairs, and 4 bonds (8 bonding electrons, half = 4): 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

questions.prompt: Which of these bonds is the most polar?
questions.explanation: Polarity follows the electronegativity difference. O–H (3.5 − 2.2 = 1.3) is larger than C–Cl (3.2 − 2.5 = 0.7), C–H (0.3), and C–C (0).

topics.title: Nomenclature
topics.concept:
IUPAC nomenclature is a systematic way to name organic molecules so that each name describes an unambiguous structure. To name an alkane, you find the longest continuous carbon chain (the parent), number it so that substituents get the lowest possible numbers, then name each substituent as a prefix and the chain as a suffix.

The root gives the number of carbons in the parent chain: meth- (1), eth- (2), prop- (3), but- (4), pent- (5), hex- (6), hept- (7), oct- (8), non- (9), dec- (10). The suffix gives the family: -ane for alkanes (all single bonds), -ene for alkenes (a C=C double bond), -yne for alkynes (a C≡C triple bond), -ol for alcohols, -al for aldehydes, -one for ketones, and -oic acid for carboxylic acids.

Substituents are named from their own carbon count with the ending -yl (methyl = CH₃–, ethyl = CH₃CH₂–, propyl = CH₃CH₂CH₂–). When a substituent appears more than once, use the prefixes di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4). Numbers (locants) tell you where each substituent or functional group sits on the chain, and substituent names are listed in alphabetical order (ignoring di-/tri- prefixes).

For example, CH₃CH₂CH₃ is propane (three carbons, saturated). CH₃CH₂OH is ethanol (two carbons plus an –OH). CH₃CH=CH₂ is propene. The branched molecule (CH₃)₂CHCH₃ has a three-carbon parent (propane) with a methyl on carbon 2, so it is 2-methylpropane.

resources.title: IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry)

questions.prompt: What is the IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has three carbons, so the root is 'prop-'. It has only single bonds, so the suffix is '-ane': propane.

questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in the parent chain of 2-methylpentane?
questions.explanation: The root 'pent-' means five carbons. The '2-methyl' is a one-carbon substituent attached to carbon 2 of that five-carbon chain.

questions.prompt: Give the IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂OH.
questions.explanation: A two-carbon chain (eth-) with an –OH group (alcohol) gives the suffix '-ol': ethanol.

questions.prompt: What does the suffix '-ene' indicate?
questions.explanation: '-ene' indicates a carbon–carbon double bond (an alkene). '-ane' = alkane, '-ol' = alcohol, '-oic acid' = carboxylic acid.

questions.prompt: What is the IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: Four carbons in a continuous chain give the root 'but-', and all single bonds give '-ane': butane.

questions.prompt: Give the IUPAC name for CH₃CH=CH₂ (a three-carbon chain with a double bond).
questions.explanation: Three carbons (prop-) plus a C=C double bond (-ene): propene. The double bond position is unambiguous here, so no locant is required.

questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms total are in 2,3-dimethylbutane?
questions.explanation: The 'butane' parent has four carbons, plus two methyl substituents (one carbon each) = six carbons total (C₆H₁₄).

questions.prompt: Which root indicates a seven-carbon chain?
questions.explanation: hept- = 7 carbons (hex- = 6, oct- = 8, non- = 9).

topics.title: Functional Groups
topics.concept:
A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic chemical reactions. Recognizing these groups is the single most important skill in organic chemistry, because molecules are classified and named by them.

The most common groups to know: an alcohol has an –OH group bonded to carbon (R–OH). A carboxylic acid has a –COOH group — a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to an –OH (R–COOH). An amine contains nitrogen bonded to carbon and/or hydrogen (R–NH₂, R₂NH, or R₃N). A ketone has a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to two carbons (R–CO–R′), while an aldehyde has the carbonyl bonded to at least one hydrogen (R–CHO). An ester has R–COO–R′ (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is also bonded to carbon), and an amide has R–CO–NR₂ (a carbonyl bonded to a nitrogen). An ether is simply an oxygen bonded to two carbons (R–O–R′), and an alkyl halide has a halogen bonded to carbon (R–X).

The difference between an aldehyde and a ketone is easy to miss: in an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon is bonded to one hydrogen and one carbon; in a ketone it is bonded to two carbons. That single hydrogen changes the naming (suffix -al vs -one) and the chemistry. Similarly, the difference between an ester and an ether is that an ester always contains a carbonyl, while an ether does not.

questions.prompt: Which functional group does CH₃COOH contain?
questions.explanation: The –COOH group is a carboxylic acid: a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to an –OH group.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between an aldehyde and a ketone?
options: Aldehydes contain nitrogen; ketones do not
The carbonyl carbon in an aldehyde is bonded to at least one hydrogen; in a ketone it is bonded to two carbons
questions.explanation: In an aldehyde (R–CHO), the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydrogen and one carbon. In a ketone (R–CO–R′), it is bonded to two carbons.

questions.prompt: Name the functional group in CH₃OH.
questions.explanation: CH₃OH has an –OH group bonded to a carbon, which is the alcohol functional group (methanol).

questions.prompt: Which of these is an amine?
questions.explanation: CH₃NH₂ contains nitrogen bonded to carbon and hydrogen — an amine. The others are an alcohol, a carboxylic acid, and a ketone.

questions.prompt: What functional group is present in CH₃COCH₃ (acetone)?
questions.explanation: Acetone has a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to two carbon atoms (one on each side), which is a ketone.

questions.prompt: Name the functional group in CH₃OCH₃.
questions.explanation: An oxygen bonded to two carbon atoms (R–O–R′) is an ether. CH₃OCH₃ is dimethyl ether.

questions.prompt: Which structure contains an ester group?
questions.explanation: An ester has the form R–COO–R′ (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is also bonded to carbon). CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl acetate) is an ester; the others are an alcohol, a ketone, and an amine.

questions.prompt: An amide group contains a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to…
questions.explanation: An amide has R–CO–NR₂: a carbonyl carbon bonded to a nitrogen atom (for example, acetamide CH₃CONH₂).

topics.title: Stereochemistry
topics.concept:
Stereochemistry is the study of how molecules are arranged in three-dimensional space. Two molecules can have the same atoms connected in the same order yet still be different, because those atoms point in different directions in space.

A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is called a chiral center (or stereocenter). A molecule with a chiral center is chiral: it is not superimposable on its mirror image, just like your left and right hands. The two mirror-image forms are enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties (boiling point, solubility) except that they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers is a racemic mixture and is optically inactive because the rotations cancel.

Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers; unlike enantiomers, diastereomers generally have different physical properties.

To name the arrangement at a chiral center, chemists use the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) rules. Assign each substituent a priority based on the atomic number of the atom directly attached to the stereocenter (higher atomic number = higher priority). Orient the lowest-priority group away from you, then trace 1 → 2 → 3: clockwise is R (rectus) and counterclockwise is S (sinister).

For alkenes, E/Z notation describes which side the higher-priority groups occupy: E (entgegen, 'opposite') means they are on opposite sides of the double bond, and Z (zusammen, 'together') means they are on the same side. A meso compound has chiral centers but also an internal mirror plane, making the whole molecule achiral.

diagram.caption: 2-Butanol — carbon 2 is a chiral center (four different groups)

questions.prompt: A carbon atom is a chiral center (stereocenter) when it is bonded to…
questions.explanation: A stereocenter is a carbon bonded to four different groups, which makes the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image.

questions.prompt: Enantiomers are best described as…
questions.explanation: Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

questions.prompt: In the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog system, the first (highest) priority is assigned to the substituent with…
questions.explanation: Priority is based on the atomic number of the atom directly attached to the stereocenter — higher atomic number means higher priority (O > N > C > H).

questions.prompt: How are diastereomers different from enantiomers?
options: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images
questions.explanation: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other, and they generally have different physical properties.

questions.prompt: In alkene E/Z notation, 'E' means the two higher-priority groups are…
options: On the same side of the double bond
On opposite sides of the double bond
Both attached to the same carbon
questions.explanation: E (from the German 'entgegen', meaning opposite) means the higher-priority group on each double-bond carbon is on the opposite side. Z ('zusammen') means the same side.

questions.prompt: How many chiral centers does 2-butanol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃) contain?
questions.explanation: Only carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups (–OH, –CH₃, –CH₂CH₃, and –H), so it is the single chiral center.

questions.prompt: A racemic mixture is…
questions.explanation: A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of enantiomers. The equal-and-opposite rotations cancel, so it is optically inactive.

questions.prompt: A meso compound is…
options: Achiral despite containing chiral centers (internal mirror plane)
questions.explanation: A meso compound contains chiral centers but also an internal plane of symmetry, which makes the overall molecule achiral and optically inactive.

topics.title: Nucleophilic Substitution (SN1 vs SN2)
topics.concept:
Nucleophilic substitution replaces a leaving group on an electrophilic carbon with a nucleophile. There are two mechanisms.

SN2 (Substitution, Nucleophilic, Bimolecular) is a single concerted step: the nucleophile attacks from the backside, 180° from the leaving group, while the leaving group departs. The rate law is rate = k[nucleophile][substrate] (second order). Because the attack comes from behind, configuration is inverted (Walden inversion). SN2 needs a strong nucleophile, a good leaving group, a polar aprotic solvent, and an unhindered substrate — reactivity follows methyl > primary > secondary, while tertiary substrates are essentially unreactive.

SN1 (Substitution, Nucleophilic, Unimolecular) is a two-step process: the leaving group departs first to form a planar carbocation (the slow, rate-determining step), then the nucleophile attacks from either face. The rate law is rate = k[substrate] (first order). The planar carbocation usually leads to racemization. SN1 requires a stable carbocation, so tertiary substrates react fastest and methyl/primary do not undergo SN1. Polar protic solvents and weak nucleophiles are fine, and carbocation rearrangements can occur.

The quick comparison: SN2 = bimolecular, concerted, inversion, prefers 1° substrates and strong nucleophiles; SN1 = unimolecular, carbocation, racemization, prefers 3° substrates and polar protic solvents.

diagram.caption: 2-Bromopropane — a secondary substrate that reacts by SN1 or SN2 depending on conditions

questions.prompt: What does 'SN2' stand for?
questions.explanation: SN2 = Substitution (one group replaces another), Nucleophilic (an electron-rich nucleophile attacks), Bimolecular (both reactants appear in the rate law).

questions.prompt: Which rate law corresponds to an SN2 reaction?
questions.explanation: SN2 is bimolecular, so the rate depends on both the nucleophile and the substrate: rate = k[Nu][RX] (second order).

questions.prompt: What is the stereochemical outcome of SN2 vs SN1?
questions.explanation: SN2 inverts configuration (backside attack). SN1 goes through a planar carbocation attacked from either face, giving racemization.

questions.prompt: A tertiary alkyl halide is most likely to undergo which substitution mechanism?
questions.explanation: Tertiary substrates form stable carbocations, so SN1 is favored. SN2 is blocked by steric hindrance from the three alkyl groups.

questions.prompt: A methyl halide with a strong nucleophile reacts by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Methyl substrates are unhindered and cannot form a stable carbocation, so they react by SN2 with a strong nucleophile.

questions.prompt: Which intermediate is formed only in SN1 (not SN2)?
questions.explanation: SN1 forms a planar carbocation after the leaving group departs. SN2 is concerted and has no carbocation — only a five-coordinate transition state.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the BEST leaving group?
questions.explanation: A good leaving group is a weak, stable base. Iodide is the weakest base listed and the best leaving group (I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻; OH⁻ and NH₂⁻ are poor).

questions.prompt: Which set of conditions favors SN2 over SN1?
questions.explanation: A strong nucleophile and a polar aprotic solvent (which leaves the nucleophile 'naked' and reactive) favor the bimolecular SN2 pathway.

topics.title: Elimination Reactions (E1 vs E2)
topics.concept:
Elimination reactions convert a substrate into an alkene by removing a leaving group and a hydrogen from an adjacent (β) carbon. There are two mechanisms.

E2 is bimolecular and concerted: a strong base removes the β-hydrogen at the same time the leaving group departs, forming the C=C double bond in one step. The rate law is rate = k[base][substrate]. E2 requires an anti-periplanar geometry — the departing hydrogen and leaving group must be 180° apart — which controls stereochemistry. With a small or unhindered base, E2 follows Zaitsev's rule and gives the more substituted (more stable) alkene. Bulky bases such as tert-butoxide (t-BuO⁻) instead give the less substituted 'Hofmann' product because they cannot easily reach the more hindered β-hydrogen.

E1 is unimolecular and stepwise. The leaving group departs first to form a carbocation (the rate-determining step, rate = k[substrate]), and then a weak base removes a β-hydrogen to form the alkene. E1 also follows Zaitsev's rule and, like SN1, can involve carbocation rearrangements. E1 competes with SN1 (both share the carbocation intermediate), while E2 competes with SN2 (both are bimolecular). Heat, a strong base, and hindered bases favor elimination, while a strong nucleophile favors substitution.

questions.prompt: What is the rate law for an E2 reaction?
questions.explanation: E2 is bimolecular: both the base and the substrate appear in the rate law, so rate = k[base][substrate] (second order).

questions.prompt: What is the rate law for an E1 reaction?
questions.explanation: E1 is unimolecular: only the substrate is in the rate law, so rate = k[substrate] (first order).

questions.prompt: Zaitsev's rule predicts that the major elimination product is…
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule: the major product is the more substituted alkene, which is more stable because alkyl groups stabilize the double bond.

questions.prompt: What geometry between the β-hydrogen and the leaving group is required for E2?
questions.explanation: E2 requires anti-periplanar geometry: the departing H and leaving group are 180° apart, which allows the forming π bond to overlap properly.

questions.prompt: Which base favors the Hofmann (less substituted) elimination product?
questions.explanation: Bulky bases such as t-BuO⁻ cannot reach the more hindered β-hydrogen, so they favor removal of the less hindered hydrogen, giving the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene.

questions.prompt: Which intermediate is formed in an E1 reaction?
questions.explanation: E1 is stepwise: the leaving group departs first to form a carbocation, then a base removes a β-hydrogen to form the alkene.

questions.prompt: E2 elimination of 2-bromobutane with a small base gives which MAJOR product?
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule favors the more substituted alkene. But-2-ene (two substituents on the double bond) is more stable than but-1-ene (one substituent).

questions.prompt: What do E1 and SN1 reactions have in common?
options: Both proceed through a carbocation intermediate
questions.explanation: E1 and SN1 share the same first step — formation of a carbocation — and both are first-order (unimolecular). They then diverge: substitution vs elimination.

topics.title: Alkene Addition Reactions
topics.concept:
Alkenes react by electrophilic addition: the π electrons of the C=C double bond attack an electrophile, and two groups add across the double bond to give a saturated product. Regiochemistry is governed by Markovnikov's rule: when HX or water adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens (the less substituted carbon), so the more substituted carbon bears the other group — because that forms the more stable carbocation.

The most important addition reactions:
• Hydrogenation (H₂ with a Pt, Pd, or Ni catalyst) adds two hydrogens in a syn fashion to give an alkane.
• Hydrohalogenation (HBr, HCl, HI) adds H and X with Markovnikov regiochemistry through a carbocation.
• Acid-catalyzed hydration (H₂O/H₂SO₄) adds water with Markovnikov regiochemistry to give an alcohol, but the carbocation can rearrange.
• Halogenation (Br₂ or Cl₂) gives a vicinal dihalide by anti addition through a cyclic halonium ion.
• Halohydrin formation (X₂ in water) places the halogen on the less substituted carbon and the OH on the more substituted carbon, with anti stereochemistry.
• Hydroboration-oxidation (BH₃ then H₂O₂/NaOH) adds water with anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry and syn stereochemistry.
• Oxymercuration-demercuration achieves Markovnikov hydration without carbocation rearrangements.

diagram.caption: Propene (CH₃CH=CH₂) — an unsymmetrical alkene used to test Markovnikov's rule

questions.prompt: Markovnikov's rule states that in HX addition to an unsymmetrical alkene…
options: The H adds to the more substituted carbon
The H adds to the less substituted carbon (more hydrogens) and X to the more substituted carbon
The X adds to the less substituted carbon
The H and X add to the same carbon
questions.explanation: Markovnikov's rule: the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (less substituted), so the halogen ends up on the more substituted carbon, via the more stable carbocation.

questions.prompt: What is the major product of adding HBr to propene (CH₃CH=CH₂)?
questions.explanation: The H adds to the terminal CH₂ carbon and Br adds to the more substituted (middle) carbon, giving 2-bromopropane (CH₃CHBrCH₃). Its common name is isopropyl bromide.

questions.prompt: Halogenation of an alkene with Br₂ gives…
options: Anti addition to form a vicinal dibromide
An alkyl bromide with Markovnikov regiochemistry
questions.explanation: Br₂ forms a cyclic bromonium ion, then bromide attacks from the opposite face, giving anti addition and a 1,2-dibromide (vicinal dibromide).

questions.prompt: Hydroboration-oxidation (BH₃ then H₂O₂/NaOH) adds water with…
questions.explanation: Hydroboration-oxidation places the OH on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov) with syn addition, because B and H add to the same face.

questions.prompt: Hydrogenation of an alkene with H₂ and a Pt/Pd/Ni catalyst produces…
questions.explanation: Hydrogenation adds H₂ across the double bond (syn addition) to give the saturated alkane.

questions.prompt: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an alkene (H₂O/H₂SO₄) proceeds through which intermediate?
questions.explanation: Protonation of the alkene forms the more stable carbocation, which water then attacks to give a Markovnikov alcohol. Rearrangement is possible.

questions.prompt: In halohydrin formation (Br₂ in water), where does the OH group end up?
questions.explanation: The bromonium ion is opened by water at the more substituted carbon (where positive charge is better stabilized), so OH adds there and Br adds to the less substituted carbon.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of oxymercuration-demercuration over acid-catalyzed hydration?
options: It achieves Markovnikov hydration without carbocation rearrangements
questions.explanation: Oxymercuration-demercuration (Hg(OAc)₂/H₂O then NaBH₄) gives Markovnikov hydration but avoids a free carbocation, so no rearrangements occur.

topics.title: SN vs E: Predicting the Mechanism
topics.concept:
Given a substrate, a reagent, and a solvent, you can predict whether substitution or elimination dominates — and which mechanism (SN1, SN2, E1, or E2) — using a few rules.

First look at the substrate. Methyl and primary substrates do not form stable carbocations, so they cannot go through SN1/E1; with a good nucleophile they react by SN2 (or E2 if the base is bulky). Tertiary substrates are too hindered for SN2, so they react by SN1/E1 with a weak base/nucleophile, or by E2 with a strong base. Secondary substrates sit in the middle and can follow any pathway depending on the reagent.

Next look at the reagent. A strong nucleophile that is a weak base (such as I⁻, Br⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, or RS⁻) favors substitution (SN2). A strong base — especially a bulky one like tert-butoxide (t-BuO⁻) — favors elimination (E2). A weak nucleophile/weak base (water, alcohols) favors the unimolecular pathways (SN1/E1).

Finally, look at conditions. Polar aprotic solvents and strong nucleophiles favor SN2; polar protic solvents favor SN1/E1. Heat favors elimination (E1/E2) because elimination increases entropy and has a larger activation energy, while lower temperature favors substitution.

A useful shorthand: strong nucleophile → substitution; strong base → elimination; weak nucleophile/base → SN1/E1; bulky base → E2; heat → elimination.

diagram.caption: tert-Butyl bromide — a 3° substrate whose pathway depends on the base and conditions

questions.prompt: A primary alkyl halide with a strong nucleophile (e.g., NaCN) in a polar aprotic solvent mainly undergoes…
questions.explanation: Primary substrates are unhindered and cannot form stable carbocations, so a strong nucleophile drives SN2.

questions.prompt: A tertiary alkyl halide treated with a strong, bulky base (t-BuOK) mainly undergoes…
questions.explanation: A bulky strong base is a poor nucleophile (steric hindrance) but a good base, so it removes a β-hydrogen and gives E2 elimination.

questions.prompt: A tertiary alkyl halide in water (a weak nucleophile/base) mainly undergoes…
questions.explanation: Tertiary substrates form stable carbocations, and a weak nucleophile/base cannot do SN2 or E2, so the reaction goes through SN1/E1.

questions.prompt: Which condition generally shifts the balance toward elimination rather than substitution?
options: A strong nucleophile that is a weak base
Heat and a strong (often bulky) base
questions.explanation: Heat favors elimination (higher entropy, higher activation energy), and a strong base removes β-hydrogens, favoring E1/E2 over substitution.

questions.prompt: A secondary alkyl halide with NaI in acetone mainly undergoes…
questions.explanation: Iodide is a strong nucleophile but a weak base, and acetone is polar aprotic, so SN2 substitution is favored over elimination.

questions.prompt: Why can't methyl and primary substrates undergo SN1 or E1?
questions.explanation: SN1/E1 require a carbocation, and methyl/primary carbocations are too unstable to form. So these substrates use SN2/E2 instead.

questions.prompt: Which type of reagent favors substitution (SN2) over elimination?
options: A strong nucleophile that is a weak base (e.g., I⁻, CN⁻)
A weak nucleophile and weak base (H₂O)
A strong base with no nucleophilicity
questions.explanation: Strong nucleophiles that are weak bases (I⁻, Br⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻) attack carbon efficiently but do not remove β-hydrogens well, favoring SN2.

questions.prompt: What is the general effect of increasing temperature on SN/E competition?
questions.explanation: Higher temperature favors elimination (E1/E2) because elimination has a larger activation energy and produces more molecules (favorable entropy).
